interview_metadata.name: Brian Martin
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: Sure, happy to. I'm Brian, I'm thirty-nine, born and raised in Florida. Grew up in a regular middle-class household in Broward County, mom and dad, one older sister. Dad was a guy who could fix anything, and a lot of who I am came from being his shadow on weekends with a socket wrench in my hand. Mom kept the house tight, packed our lunches, kept the budget on a little legal pad on the kitchen counter. Went through public school in Pompano, played a lot of pickup ball, fished off the pier, the usual Florida kid stuff. Graduated high school in '05 and honestly thought I'd go straight into a trade program, but life had other ideas. I worked construction off and on through my twenties, did some auto work, bounced around a bit. Met my wife, Megan, at a friend's barbecue in 2010, married her in 2013, and we've got two kids now, a boy and a girl. About three years back I hurt my back pretty good on a job site, and that knocked me out of full-time work. Since then I've been the at-home parent essentially, running the household, doing handyman jobs for neighbors, volunteering at the senior center over on McNab Road. Right now I'm trying to get certified for home energy retrofits so I can put a real business together, something steady that doesn't put me back on a ladder ten hours a day. That's the short version, I guess.

follow_ups.question: What part of growing up in Broward County stuck with you the most?
follow_ups.response: The water. Honestly, just being close to the ocean. Saturday mornings my dad and I'd drive down to Pompano Pier before sunrise and just fish, talk, not talk. That rhythm got into me. I still walk the beach almost every morning.

follow_ups.question: How did you and Megan end up together?
follow_ups.response: Buddy of mine, Tony, threw a Memorial Day cookout in 2010 over in Coconut Creek. She was his cousin's roommate. We ended up talking about the Red Sox of all things, because she grew up outside Boston before her family moved south. That was kind of it. Three years later I proposed at the same beach my dad used to take me to.

follow_ups.question: How's the back injury changed how you see your future?
follow_ups.response: Forced me to stop pretending I'd be swinging a hammer at sixty. I had to get smarter about how I make a dollar. That's why the retrofit certification matters so much, it's brains over back.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: Yeah, probably the back injury, summer of 2023. I was working a framing job over in Coral Springs and a stack of plywood slid off a pallet and caught me sideways. Two herniated discs. I spent a couple months on the couch, couldn't even pick up my daughter. The crossroads was, do I go back to the same kind of work and just push through, or do I rebuild what I do for a living. Megan and I sat at the kitchen table one night with a yellow pad, listed every skill I had, and decided I'd stay home with the kids, pick up neighborhood handyman jobs, and study for a certification I could actually use long-term. That conversation reshaped the whole household. Money got tighter, but the kids see me every day now, and I'm planning something that's actually mine.

follow_ups.question: Was the decision hard for you as a guy who was used to being the breadwinner?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, it stung. I grew up thinking my job was to provide, full stop. Took me a while to see that being there for the kids and running the house is providing too. My dad actually told me that, which surprised me coming from him.

follow_ups.question: Did anything good come out of it you didn't expect?
follow_ups.response: My relationship with my son. He's seven now. We cook together, we work on the old Camaro in the garage on Saturdays. I wouldn't have had that if I was still gone twelve hours a day.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: Conscious choice. Definitely conscious. Megan and I literally wrote it down on a legal pad. I'm a planner by nature, so leaving something that big to chance wasn't going to happen.

follow_ups.question: Do you usually plan that thoroughly?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, almost to a fault. I keep a notebook for the household budget, I keep one for jobs, one for the kids' school stuff. Megan teases me about it.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Honestly, yeah. Workers' comp was a nightmare, took eight months to settle a claim that should've taken two. If there'd been a real local nonprofit that helped tradespeople navigate that paperwork, I'd have saved a lot of stress and probably a couple thousand dollars.

follow_ups.question: Did you reach out to anyone for help?
follow_ups.response: Mostly family and a guy from my old crew who'd been through something similar. No formal support.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: Yeah, my wife Megan, she's thirty-seven, works as a dental hygienist over at a practice on Sample Road. We've been married twelve years this October. We have two kids: Tyler is seven, going into second grade, and Hannah just turned four, she's in pre-K. Both of them are at the age where they're sponges, into everything. My parents are still around, mom and dad both retired, they live about twenty minutes north in Boca. My sister Karen is up in Jacksonville with her husband and three kids, we see them maybe twice a year and talk on the phone every couple of weeks. Megan's family is mostly up in Massachusetts, so we make a trip up there every summer if we can swing it. Family is honestly the engine of everything. Sunday dinners at our house with my parents are kind of a standing thing, Megan does a roast, I do the sides, and the kids run wild in the yard.

follow_ups.question: How would you describe your relationship with your wife?
follow_ups.response: Solid. She's the steady one when I get spun up about money or work. I'm the one who keeps her laughing when her shifts at the office get heavy. We're a real team, especially after the injury.

follow_ups.question: What's the best part about being a dad to Tyler and Hannah?
follow_ups.response: Watching them figure stuff out. Tyler is starting to actually catch a softball without flinching, and Hannah is in a phase where she narrates everything. They keep me out of my own head.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your folks?
follow_ups.response: Every Sunday, basically. Mom calls me on Wednesdays too, like clockwork.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: Just my brother-in-law Mike, Megan's brother, he lives in Tampa. We're tight, we go fishing whenever I can get over there.

follow_ups.question: What do you guys usually fish for?
follow_ups.response: Snook mostly, sometimes redfish in the flats. He has a little flats boat.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: Yeah, a few. Tony, the guy who threw the barbecue where I met Megan, he's basically a brother to me at this point. He runs a small roofing crew in Margate, we talk every couple days. Then there's the softball guys, our spring league at Mitchell Moore Park, probably eight or nine of us who've played together five, six years now. And the senior center crew, there are a couple of older volunteers I've gotten really close to, especially this guy Walter who's eighty-two and still sharper than me on a chessboard. We do bingo nights together every other Thursday.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see Tony?
follow_ups.response: At least once a week. Either he's at our place watching a game or I'm helping him with something at his.

follow_ups.question: How did you start at the senior center?
follow_ups.response: After the injury I needed something to do that wasn't sitting on the couch. A neighbor mentioned they needed help with event setup. Showed up once, never really left.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: We're in Pompano Beach, the 33063 zip, which is sort of the western, more residential side, off of Atlantic Boulevard. It's a mix of single-family homes built in the seventies and eighties, lots of working families, lots of retirees, a good chunk of Caribbean and Latino families too. Our street is quiet, palm trees, a couple of kids Tyler's age two doors down. There's a little plaza about a mile away with a Publix, a Cuban place we love, and a hardware store I'm at probably twice a week. The beach is about a fifteen-minute drive east. It's not fancy, but it's real, you know? Neighbors actually wave at each other.

follow_ups.question: How long have you been in this house?
follow_ups.response: Six years. We bought it in 2020 when the rates were still good, thank God.

follow_ups.question: What do you like best about the area?
follow_ups.response: The mix of people. The kids hear three languages on the block. And the food, you can get authentic Haitian, Cuban, Jamaican within a five-minute drive.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: Mostly safe. There was a stretch a couple years ago with some car break-ins, somebody got into my truck and took my tools, that was rough. But I put up a couple cameras, we have a neighborhood group chat now, and it's been quiet since. Day to day I feel fine.

follow_ups.question: Do the kids play outside?
follow_ups.response: Front yard with me out there, yeah. Tyler rides his bike up and down the street.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: Ups are the climate, the beach, the diversity, the cost compared to where my wife's family is up north. Downs are the heat in August, the insurance going through the roof after the hurricane seasons, and traffic. Traffic on University Drive is its own little hell.

follow_ups.question: Has insurance hit you hard?
follow_ups.response: Our homeowner's went up almost forty percent over two renewals. It's a real conversation in our budget.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Just the four of us: me, Megan, Tyler, Hannah. And our dog, a lab mix named Biscuit, but I don't think she counts for your form. No roommates, no in-laws staying over right now.

follow_ups.question: How old is Biscuit?
follow_ups.response: She's six. We got her right before Hannah was born, which in hindsight was ambitious.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: All permanent.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: My parents stay over on holidays. That's about it.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, nobody.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Weekdays look pretty similar. I'm up at five-thirty, walk on the beach for about forty minutes, back home by quarter past seven. Get the kids fed and Tyler off to school by eight. Hannah's pre-K is half-day, so I drop her at nine and pick her up at noon. Between drop-offs I'll run handyman jobs for neighbors, work on the certification coursework, or run the household stuff, laundry, grocery, that kind of thing. Afternoons are kid time, homework with Tyler, garden with Hannah. Megan gets home around six, we eat together, kids in bed by eight-thirty, and I usually study or watch a Sox game until about ten. Weekends I'm either at the senior center Saturday morning, fishing or working on the Camaro Saturday afternoon, and church-or-family-day Sunday.

follow_ups.question: What kind of handyman jobs are you doing right now?
follow_ups.response: Small stuff. Fixing a busted disposal for the lady across the street, hanging shelves, replacing a porch light, the kind of jobs that take an hour or two and pay enough to cover groceries that week.

follow_ups.question: Are weekends sacred?
follow_ups.response: Saturday afternoon with my son is sacred. Everything else flexes.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: Right now I'm classified as not in the workforce because of the back, but I do informal handyman work, cash mostly, maybe ten to fifteen hours a week spread across neighbors. I'm also volunteering about eight hours a week at the Northeast Focal Point Senior Center, leading rec games on Tuesdays and helping with event logistics. And I'm putting in about ten hours a week studying for the BPI Building Analyst certification, that's the home energy retrofit credential.

follow_ups.question: When did you start the certification work?
follow_ups.response: About four months ago. I sit at the kitchen table with the laptop after the kids go down.

follow_ups.question: What's your goal timeline?
follow_ups.response: I want to test by end of the year and have a real business filed with the state by next spring.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I do all the household budgeting, that's a Sunday-night ritual with a spreadsheet I built. I'm the primary cook three or four nights a week. I take Biscuit to the vet, handle the cars, manage the home repairs, and I'm the one who deals with Tyler's school stuff, teacher conferences and all that. Megan handles the kids' medical appointments and most of the social stuff with her side of the family.

follow_ups.question: How do you split things up?
follow_ups.response: Pretty naturally these days. After the injury we kind of rebalanced based on what I could physically do and what made sense. It works.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: Big one was starting the BPI coursework, that's added two hours a night basically. The other one is Hannah moved from full-time daycare to half-day pre-K in August, so I'm picking her up at noon now, which actually killed my midday job window, which has been a tradeoff.

follow_ups.question: Are you finding the time for the coursework?
follow_ups.response: Barely. I'm tired. But it's the path forward so I'm sticking with it.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: Tyler's up at seven, breakfast usually scrambled eggs and toast, in the car by seven-forty, at his elementary off Sample Road by eight. School till two-thirty. I pick him up, he has a snack, homework first, then he can play. He does little league baseball in the spring, practices Tuesdays and Thursdays, and karate on Wednesday evenings. Hannah's pre-K is nine to noon, then she's home with me, naps from one to two-thirty, then we usually go to the park or work in the garden. Bath at seven, books at seven-thirty, lights out by eight.

follow_ups.question: How's Tyler doing in school?
follow_ups.response: Reading's a little behind, math he's ahead. We work on reading every night, twenty minutes minimum.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: Nothing big. A couple speeding tickets in my twenties, one when I was rushing to a job site on I-95, deserved it. After the truck break-in I dealt with Broward Sheriff to file a report, they were professional but realistic, told me straight up they probably wouldn't recover the tools. Other than that, the deputies do drive-throughs on our street sometimes, friendly waves.

follow_ups.question: How do you generally feel about local law enforcement?
follow_ups.response: Mostly fine. I think they have a tough job. I'm aware not everyone has the same experience I do.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: Just the break-in report. I remember being more frustrated with the insurance side than with the deputies. Nothing stands out negatively.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: A cousin on my dad's side did some time for a DUI back in maybe 2012. That was hard on the family. Nobody in my immediate household, no.

follow_ups.question: How's your cousin doing now?
follow_ups.response: He's clean and working in Pensacola. We don't talk much but I'm glad he turned it around.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote in the big ones, presidential and the midterms. Local stuff, school board, city commission, I've been getting better about it the last couple cycles because of the kids. Megan's the one who keeps me on top of the local races.

follow_ups.question: Do you vote early or on election day?
follow_ups.response: Early voting, usually the Saturday before. Less lines, and I don't trust the mail for ballots, just personal preference.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I'd call myself a moderate, leaning conservative on some things, leaning the other way on others. I grew up in a household that voted Republican pretty consistently, traditional Florida coastal values, self-reliance, smaller government. As I've gotten older, though, especially after the injury and seeing what insurance and workers' comp actually look like for working people, I've gotten more sympathetic to the idea that there ought to be a better safety net. I'm pro-Second Amendment, I'm pro-trade, I think public schools need real funding, I think hurricane preparedness and climate are real and need attention, especially down here. I'm tired of both parties to be honest. I voted for who I thought was the steadier hand last cycle, not necessarily because I loved them. I try not to get sucked into the cable news circus, it makes my anxiety worse.

follow_ups.question: Where do you get most of your political information?
follow_ups.response: Local newspaper online, the Sun Sentinel. NPR in the car sometimes. I avoid Twitter, it's a nightmare.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk politics with friends?
follow_ups.response: Not much. Tony and I disagree on a lot of stuff and we just don't go there. Too much to lose.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: Yeah, like I said, the injury moved me. I used to be more, pull yourself up by your bootstraps, and I still believe in personal responsibility, but I've seen up close how a single bad day can financially level a family. So healthcare access and disability support matter more to me now. Also climate, after seeing two of the last four hurricane seasons, I can't pretend that's not real anymore. Insurance companies sure aren't pretending.

follow_ups.question: Has any of that strained relationships?
follow_ups.response: A little with my dad, who's pretty set in his views. We've learned to talk about the Sox instead.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: Somewhat. I'm a white guy, I haven't lived it, so I try to listen more than I talk. I have neighbors and friends who've had very different experiences with police than I have, and that's stuck with me. I don't agree with every tactic of the movement, the property damage stuff was hard to watch, but I think the core point that the system doesn't treat everyone the same is pretty clearly true.

follow_ups.question: Has it changed how you raise your kids?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, we talk to Tyler about treating everyone the same, and we don't tolerate slurs in our house, period.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the core question, is policing fair across communities, is a legitimate one that deserves an honest look. I've also got friends who are deputies and I know most of them are good people doing a stressful job. So for me it's not pick a side, it's how do we get to a system that's actually fair and accountable, with cops who feel supported and communities that feel protected. I don't pretend I have the answer.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think we've made progress, and I think we've still got real ground to cover. Living in Broward, you can't really pretend race doesn't shape people's day-to-day. I want my kids to grow up in a country where they're judged on what they do, not what they look like, and I think that means white folks like me have to do some of the listening work, even when it's uncomfortable.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: Mostly conversations at home and with close friends. Haven't gone to a protest. I've spoken up a couple times when a buddy said something that crossed a line at a cookout. Small stuff.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: Mixed bag. Megan is probably a little more progressive on it than I am, she's pushed me to listen more. My dad mostly thinks the media blows it up. My sister, who teaches up in Jacksonville, has gotten more vocal. So there's a real range, even in one family.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall, decent for thirty-nine. The big thing is my back, two herniated discs at L4 and L5 from the 2023 injury. I manage it with stretching, physical therapy exercises every morning, and being careful with how I lift. I also have some chronic anxiety, which I've had since my twenties really, that I manage mostly through routine and exercise. Blood pressure's borderline high, doctor wants me to drop fifteen pounds. Otherwise I'm reasonably healthy, no diabetes, no big stuff.

follow_ups.question: Are you on any meds for the anxiety?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, I take a low dose of sertraline. It takes the edge off without making me feel flat.

follow_ups.question: What does the morning stretching look like?
follow_ups.response: Fifteen minutes of physical therapy moves, planks, glute bridges, that kind of thing. I do them before the beach walk.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: Easy is the climate, you can walk outside year-round, and being home with the kids means I cook more, so I control what we eat. Hard is the stress of the financial situation, that's what fuels the anxiety and the bad sleep, and honestly the temptation to drink a beer or two at night to unwind. I try to keep that in check.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: The back injury in summer of 2023 was the main event, herniated discs, MRI, physical therapy, the whole deal. I had a flare-up last winter where I couldn't get out of bed for three days, that was scary. Otherwise, my anxiety got bad enough in early 2024 that I went back on medication after being off it for years.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: Yeah, the back is the obvious one, I can't do framing or roofing anymore, that ended my career path. With the kids it limits the rough-and-tumble, I can't toss Hannah in the air like I used to, that bums me out a little.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: My dad had a minor heart attack in 2022, mild, but it scared all of us. He's on meds now, watches his diet, and he's doing well. Mom has some arthritis but nothing serious. The kids have been healthy, knock on wood.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: We're on Megan's insurance through the dental practice, which is okay but not great. Deductibles are high. I've put off MRI follow-ups for my back because of cost. We've never delayed care for the kids, that's a hard line for us. I also skipped a dental procedure last year that probably needs doing.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: I've done acupuncture for the back, it actually helped some. Megan's into essential oils a little, lavender for sleep, that kind of thing. We're not super alternative, but we're not closed off to it either.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I quit smoking in 2015, was about a half-pack-a-day guy. Drinking, I'll have two or three beers in an evening, maybe four or five nights a week. After the injury that crept up and Megan called me on it, so I've pulled it back. I don't drink hard liquor at home.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I was on opioids for about six weeks after the injury, hydrocodone, and I made myself stop because I could feel how easy it would be to keep going. Now I take ibuprofen when the back acts up. Marijuana, very occasionally, an edible if my back is really seizing up. Last time was maybe two months ago.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: Megan's employer insurance covers the basics. We have an HSA we contribute to when we can. Big expenses go on a credit card and we pay them down over a few months. It's manageable but it's a real chunk of the budget.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: Pro-vaccination. The kids are fully up to date. Megan and I got the COVID vaccines and the flu shot every year. I trust our pediatrician on that stuff.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: Our pediatrician for the kids, and my general practitioner for me. I'll glance at CDC stuff sometimes. I don't trust random Facebook posts on this one.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: Honestly, mixed. There's been real joy, watching the kids grow, getting closer to Megan, the certification path opening up. There's also been a steady hum of anxiety underneath it about money, about whether the business is going to actually work, about whether I'll be a strong enough provider. I sleep about six hours a night when I should be getting eight. But I'm not in a dark place. I'd call it cautiously hopeful with a side of constant low-grade worry.

transcript.question_text: Tell me a story about a time in the last year when you were in a rough place or struggling emotionally.
transcript.response: Around February, the homeowner's insurance renewal came in higher than expected, and at the same time my back flared and I had to cancel a couple jobs. For about a week I felt like I was failing my family. Megan caught me crying in the garage one night. We talked, made a new plan, and I scheduled an extra session with my therapist. That helped reset things.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they struggle with depression, anxiety, or something else like that. How about for you?
transcript.response: Generalized anxiety, yeah, diagnosed in my late twenties. I see a therapist about once a month, take the sertraline, and exercise is probably the biggest tool. When I skip the morning walk I can feel the difference by afternoon.

transcript.question_text: How has it been for your family?
transcript.response: Megan has her own stress from work, dental hygiene is harder on the body than people realize. The kids are kids, happy and bouncing off the walls. My mom worries about everything, that's where I got it from probably.

transcript.question_text: Some people say that religion or spirituality is important in their lives, for others not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: Yeah, somewhat. I was raised Southern Baptist, my parents are still pretty active. As an adult I've kind of softened into more of a generally Christian, non-denominational thing. We attend a community church here in Pompano maybe two Sundays a month. The kids do Sunday school. I pray, more like a conversation in my head than anything formal, especially during the anxiety stuff. I wouldn't call myself super devout but faith is a real part of how I make sense of things.

follow_ups.question: What draws you to your current church?
follow_ups.response: The pastor's down to earth, the community is welcoming, and they actually do real volunteer work in the area. Not a lot of show.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they use Facebook, Instagram, or other social media to stay connected with the wider world. How about for you? Tell me all about how you use these types of platforms.
transcript.response: Facebook mostly, to keep up with family up north and to coordinate the softball league. I post photos of the kids occasionally. Instagram I have but rarely use, mostly for my photography, the coastal wildlife stuff. I'm in a couple of neighborhood groups on Facebook, that's actually useful for the handyman work, people post asking for recommendations. I don't do Twitter or TikTok. I'm too old for that.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they use Facebook or Twitter to get (emotional or financial) support during tough times. What about you?
transcript.response: Not really. I keep that stuff offline. If I'm having a hard time, I talk to Megan, Tony, or my therapist. Not Facebook.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your level of stress, worry, and your emotional coping strategies.
transcript.response: Stress has been up the last six months because of the certification push and the insurance situation. I've leaned harder into the morning walks and added one more therapy session a month. Trying to drink less, sleep more.

transcript.question_text: This might be repetitive, but before we go on to the next section, I want to quickly make sure I have this right: who are you living with right now?
transcript.response: Megan, my wife. Tyler, seven. Hannah, four. And Biscuit the dog.

transcript.question_text: Any babies or small children?
transcript.response: Hannah's four, so still small, but no babies.

transcript.question_text: Anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Any lodgers, boarders, or employees who live here?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Who shares the responsibility for the rent, mortgage, or other household expenses?
transcript.response: Megan and me, joint.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to talk about how you make ends meet and what the monthly budget looks like for you and your family. What were your biggest expenses last month?
transcript.response: Mortgage was about eighteen-fifty. Groceries ran around nine hundred for the four of us. Homeowner's and car insurance combined hit about six hundred. Utilities maybe three-fifty. Hannah's pre-K is four hundred. Gas, another two hundred.

transcript.question_text: How much did your household spend in the past month? Is that the usual amount? And if not, how much do you usually spend and on what?
transcript.response: About fifty-two hundred last month, which was a little higher than usual because we had a car repair. Usual is closer to forty-eight hundred.

transcript.question_text: Does your household own or rent your home?
transcript.response: Own, with a mortgage. Bought in 2020.

transcript.question_text: Bills can fluctuate over the course of a year. Seasons change, there are holidays and special events, school starts and ends, and so on. Tell me all about how your bills have fluctuated over the past year.
transcript.response: Summer power bills are a killer in Florida, you can run two-fifty to three-fifty a month with the AC. Holidays in December always run us about a thousand extra between gifts and travel. Back to school in August was about four hundred in supplies and clothes for the kids. Insurance renewals hit hard in February and June. Other than that, pretty steady.

transcript.question_text: Tell me all about how you coped with any extra expenses in the past months.
transcript.response: Credit card mostly, then paid down over two or three months. I picked up an extra handyman job here and there. Megan worked a couple Saturdays for overtime.

transcript.question_text: Some people have a savings account, some people save in a different way, and some people say they don't save. How about you?
transcript.response: We have a savings account at our credit union, currently about thirty-two hundred in it, which is light. We also have a small Roth IRA Megan started before we got married, maybe eleven thousand. And the HSA. We're not where we want to be, but we save what we can.

transcript.question_text: Some people save for big things, like a home, while others save for a rainy day. How about for you (in the last year)?
transcript.response: Rainy day. We've been trying to build up to a real three-month emergency fund. We had a bigger cushion before the injury, used a lot of it during the recovery period. Now we're rebuilding.

transcript.question_text: Some people have student loans or credit card debt. Others take out loans from family or friends or find other ways of borrowing money. Tell me about all the debts you're paying on right now.
transcript.response: Mortgage, about two-twenty left on it. One car loan, about eight thousand on Megan's car. Credit cards float between three and five thousand at any given time. No student loans. No family loans, I won't do that.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any time during the past year that you haven't had enough money to buy something that you needed or pay a bill that was due.
transcript.response: Last February, the insurance renewal and a plumbing repair hit in the same week. We pushed a credit card payment by ten days and ate a late fee. Hated it but we got through it.

transcript.question_text: What is or was your occupation? In this occupation, what kind of work do you do and what are the most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My main career was residential construction, specifically framing and finish carpentry. I worked for a couple of contractors in Broward, did some independent jobs. Important activities were reading blueprints, framing walls, installing trim, sometimes leading a two or three person crew on smaller projects. Currently I'm doing informal handyman work and pursuing the BPI Building Analyst certification so I can move into home energy auditing and retrofits.

transcript.question_text: Was your occupation covered by a union or employee association contract?
transcript.response: No, non-union. Most residential construction down here isn't.

transcript.question_text: In the past year, how many weeks did you work (for a few hours, including paid vacation, paid sick leave, and military service)?
transcript.response: If you count the informal handyman work, probably forty weeks. Formal employment, zero.

transcript.question_text: How many hours each week did you usually work?
transcript.response: Ten to fifteen hours of paid work most weeks.

transcript.question_text: In the past week, did you work for pay (even for 1 hour) at a job or business?
transcript.response: Yeah, fixed a neighbor's garbage disposal and hung some shelves. Maybe four hours total.

transcript.question_text: Did you have more than one job or business, including part time, evening, or weekend work?
transcript.response: Just the handyman work, all under one informal umbrella.

transcript.question_text: Now, in the past month, how many jobs did you work, including part time, evening, or weekend work?
transcript.response: About seven or eight small jobs for different neighbors.

transcript.question_text: For your job or occupations, how much money did you receive in the past month?
transcript.response: Maybe eight hundred dollars in cash from handyman work last month.

transcript.question_text: How often do you get paid?
transcript.response: Per job, usually same day, cash or Venmo.

transcript.question_text: In total, how much did your household make in the past month?
transcript.response: Megan netted about thirty-eight hundred. Plus my eight hundred. So around forty-six hundred for the month.

transcript.question_text: Switching gears a bit, let's talk a little about tax time. Did you file taxes last year (the most recent year)?
transcript.response: Yes, joint return. I used H&R Block online, got it done in late February.

transcript.question_text: Tell me more about your workplace. How long have you been at your current job? How would you describe the benefits that come with your job? (This could include things like health benefits, paid time off, vacation, and sick time.)
transcript.response: No current employer, so no benefits on my side. Megan's been at her dental practice for nine years, decent health coverage, two weeks paid vacation, five sick days.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your relationships at work? (How is your relationship with your manager or boss? How are your relationships with your coworkers?)
transcript.response: For me, the neighbors are basically my clients and they're great. Megan likes her coworkers, her boss is fine but stingy with raises.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about how predictable your work schedule is. How would you describe your job in terms of flexibility with your hours?
transcript.response: Mine is totally flexible by design, I schedule jobs around the kids. Megan's is fixed, Monday through Thursday, seven to four, plus every other Friday morning.

transcript.question_text: Some people say it's hard to take or keep a job because of child care. How about for you?
transcript.response: Huge factor. That's a big reason I'm the one home with the kids, daycare for both would eat most of what I could earn back at framing.

transcript.question_text: Do you receive any payments or benefits from SNAP, food stamps, housing voucher payments, supplemental security income, or any other programs like that?
transcript.response: No, nothing like that. We looked into SNAP after the injury but we were just over the line.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about times over the last year when your income was especially low. And tell me about all the things you did to make ends meet during that time.
transcript.response: December was light because nobody wants a stranger in their house over the holidays. We dipped into savings, I cut my own beer budget, we did a really modest Christmas, just the kids really. We made it work.

transcript.question_text: What would it be like for you if you had to spend $400 for an emergency? Would you have the money, and if not, how would you get it?
transcript.response: Yeah, we'd have it in the savings account. It would sting but we could cover it without a credit card.

transcript.question_text: Overall, how do you feel about your financial situation?
transcript.response: Stable but stretched. We're not behind, we're not going hungry, but we don't have the cushion I'd like and one bad month can move things around quickly. I feel like we're building back, but it's slow. The certification is the bet I'm making on improving it.

transcript.question_text: Are you now married, widowed, divorced, separated, or have you never been married? If you are not currently married, are you currently living with a romantic partner?
transcript.response: Married. Twelve years this October.

transcript.question_text: For our records, we also need your date of birth. Could you please provide that?
Were you born in the United States? If you were not born in the U.S., what country were you born, and what year did you first come to the U.S. to live?
transcript.response: Yes, born in the U.S.

transcript.question_text: What city and state were you born in?
transcript.response: Fort Lauderdale, Florida.

transcript.question_text: Are you of Hispanic, Latinx, or Spanish origin?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: What race or races do you identify with?
transcript.response: White, Anglo-American.

transcript.question_text: What is the highest degree or grade you've completed?
transcript.response: High school diploma.

transcript.question_text: Are you enrolled in school?
transcript.response: Not in a degree program. I'm self-studying for the BPI certification.

transcript.question_text: Have you been enrolled in school during the past 3 months?
transcript.response: No, not formally.

transcript.question_text: Have you ever served on active duty in the U.S. Armed Forces, Reserves, or National Guard?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: What religion do you identify with, if any?
transcript.response: Christian, non-denominational, raised Southern Baptist.

transcript.question_text: Generally speaking, do you usually think of yourself as a Democrat, a Republican, an Independent, or what? And how strongly do you associate with that party?
transcript.response: Independent, but historically leaning Republican. I'd call it weak association, I vote the candidate more than the party.

transcript.question_text: Do you think of yourself as closer to the Democratic Party or to the Republican Party?
transcript.response: Slightly closer to Republican on traditional values and fiscal stuff, but on healthcare and climate I'm closer to the Democrats. Probably overall a hair to the right of center.

transcript.question_text: What was the city and state that you lived in when you were 16 years old?
transcript.response: Coral Springs, Florida.

transcript.question_text: Did you live with both your own mother and father when you were 16?
transcript.response: Yes, both parents and my older sister.

transcript.question_text: Who else did you live with?
transcript.response: Just my sister Karen, no one else.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your dad completed?
transcript.response: High school, plus a vocational welding certificate.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your mom completed?
transcript.response: Two years of community college.

transcript.question_text: Did your mom work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, off and on.

transcript.question_text: What was her job? What kind of work did she do? What were her most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: She was a receptionist at a pediatric office for years, scheduling appointments, billing, handling parents on the phone, that kind of thing.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did she work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where she worked?
transcript.response: A pediatric medical office in Coral Springs, three doctors, healthcare for kids basically.

transcript.question_text: Did your dad work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, always.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: He was a welder for a structural steel company. Read drawings, MIG and stick welding, fabricated steel for commercial buildings.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: A structural steel fabricator in Pompano. They made steel beams and assemblies for commercial construction projects around South Florida.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: Five years from now I hope I've passed the BPI cert and have a real little business going, Martin Home Energy or something, two or three steady contracts a month, enough to put real money in savings. I want the kids healthy and doing well in school, Tyler hitting the ball, Hannah reading on her own. I want Megan to be able to drop to four days a week. I'd love to take that sailing trip to the Azores with my brother-in-law. And I want my back to be stable enough to walk the beach with Megan when we're sixty.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: Family, full stop. Megan and the kids. After that, integrity, doing what I say I'll do, showing up for people. And community, being someone the neighbors and the senior center can count on. The rest is detail.

summaries.demographer: Brian Martin is a 39-year-old white, non-Hispanic male, married 12 years to Megan with two young children (Tyler, 7; Hannah, 4), residing as a homeowner in Pompano Beach, FL 33063 (Q05, Q08, Q58, Q84, Q89). He holds a high school diploma and is currently out of the formal labor force following a 2023 disabling work injury, performing informal handyman work and pursuing a BPI Building Analyst credential (Q16, Q33, Q90, Q91). Household income (~$4,600/mo) is primarily from his wife's nine-year tenure as a dental hygienist, with the family covered under her employer health insurance (Q40, Q74, Q76). He represents a familiar life-course profile: working-class tradesman absorbed into the at-home-parent role after a midlife health shock, with intergenerational continuity (welder father, pediatric-office-receptionist mother) (Q103, Q106).
summaries.behavioral_economist: Brian exhibits strong planning orientation and loss aversion: he keeps multiple paper notebooks, runs a Sunday spreadsheet review, and explicitly built his post-injury pivot around a written legal-pad decision (Q03, Q17, Q02). He is risk-averse around debt (refuses family loans, paid off his only major credit-card balances over months) yet willing to make calculated long-horizon investments such as ~10 hours/week studying for BPI certification with no near-term payoff (Q16, Q63). His incentive structure heavily weights childcare-cost-vs-wage tradeoffs, having explicitly concluded that returning to framing would not net more than current handyman income net of daycare for two (Q79). Peer influence is moderate and channel-specific: he relies on a tight in-person network (wife, Tony, therapist) over social-media support, and his consumption is steered by Megan as a stabilizing partner (Q49, Q44).
summaries.political_scientist: Brian is a weakly-affiliated Independent who has historically leaned Republican but has migrated toward the political center post-injury, citing personal experience with workers' comp and homeowner-insurance fragility as having softened his self-reliance ideology toward greater openness on healthcare and climate (Q24, Q25, Q95, Q96). Civic engagement is robust at the local-community level (volunteers ~8 hrs/week at Northeast Focal Point Senior Center, active in neighborhood Facebook group, joins community church) but moderate at the formal-electoral level (votes consistently in presidentials, increasingly in local races due to children) (Q01, Q16, Q23, Q47). Institutional trust is selective: high for personal physicians, local newspaper, and NPR; low for cable news, Twitter, mail-in ballots, and the workers' compensation bureaucracy (Q04, Q24, Q42). On race, he positions himself as a sympathetic-but-cautious white moderate who listens more than speaks, declines protest activity, and emphasizes accountable-yet-supported policing (Q26, Q27, Q29).
summaries.psychologist: Brian presents as a conscientious, agreeable, sociable individual with a meaningful trait-level neuroticism load expressed as diagnosed generalized anxiety since his late twenties, currently managed with sertraline, monthly therapy, daily exercise, and ritualized routines (Q31, Q43, Q45). His self-concept is anchored in provider-and-fixer identity that was destabilized by the 2023 back injury and is being actively reconstructed around an at-home-parent + small-business-founder narrative, with explicit cognitive reframing assistance from his father and wife (Q02, Q34). Coping is approach-oriented and structured (planning, walking, talking to wife/therapist/best friend Tony) rather than avoidant, though he acknowledges a recent uptick in alcohol use that Megan flagged and he reduced (Q38, Q49, Q50). Relational style is securely attached and high-disclosure within a small circle, with strong generativity drives toward children, mentorship of younger volunteers, and community service that align coherently with stated terminal values of family, integrity, and reliability (Q07, Q108, Q109).
